title: UNIQUE: one row per distinct value

screens.prompt: In B8, count how many different couriers appear in A2:A7 by collapsing the list with UNIQUE.

hints.syntax: =COUNTA(UNIQUE(A2:A7)): one pair of brackets for UNIQUE, one for COUNTA.
hints.func-unique: UNIQUE collapses the six courier rows to the distinct names. Counting them by hand works once, then a new delivery arrives.
hints.require-ref: Point UNIQUE at the courier column A2:A7. The deliveries in B2:B7 are six different numbers.
hints.value: That is not the number of couriers. UNIQUE hands back a block of cells, and COUNTA is what turns the block into 3.
hints.error: #NAME? means this Excel build has no UNIQUE. #N/A means exactly_once left nothing to return, and #VALUE! means the third argument was not TRUE or FALSE.

reject.why: TRUE in the second slot is by_col, not exactly_once, so all six deliveries come back
exactly_once keeps only values that appear once, so only Crane survives
range stops mid-list, so Nordic is never seen
counts the six delivery rows instead of the distinct couriers
types the arithmetic instead of collapsing the list
collapses the deliveries column, which has six distinct numbers
divides the correct count by zero

docs.explain:
UNIQUE reads a range and returns one copy of each distinct value, in the order it first met them. In A2:A7, Swift appears three times, Nordic twice and Crane once, so UNIQUE(A2:A7) gives Swift, Nordic, Crane.

The exercise wants a count, so the block is wrapped: =COUNTA(UNIQUE(A2:A7)) counts the rows it occupies and returns 3 in B8. The third argument, exactly_once, changes the meaning. Set it to TRUE and only values that appear a single time come back, which here leaves Crane alone.

A block needs empty cells to land in. If one of them is already occupied, the formula returns #SPILL! and names the cell in the way. Excel leaves the neighbouring data where it is. UNIQUE alone needs three rows here, so leave a few blanks under anything that returns a block.

errors.text: The result needs three rows and one of them holds something else, so Excel stops and names the cell in the way.
exactly_once returned nothing because no courier appears a single time, leaving the block empty.
The workbook's version of Excel predates dynamic arrays, so UNIQUE does not exist there.

docs.atWork: A courier list that grows every week, and the dropdown fed from it without retyping the names.
docs.outcome: Count the distinct couriers in a column without retyping the list.

seo.title: UNIQUE in Excel: one row per distinct value
seo.description: UNIQUE spills one row per distinct value in the order it met them, and COUNTA counts that block. The third argument returns only values that appear once.
